title: Eight Weeks After the Church Hurt You
subtitle: An eight week plan from James Bell for anyone hurt by a church or by people who spoke for God. Safety first, the Psalms' words for betrayal, and no hurry back through any church door.
intro:
This is an eight week walk for the person a church hurt, whether it was a pastor or leader you trusted, a congregation that closed ranks when you spoke up, or a church that chose its reputation over the truth. Each week holds one focus, one small daily practice, one thing to read, one tool to use, and one honest question. It moves slowly on purpose, from naming what happened and bringing it to God in lament, through telling the truth to someone safe and telling Christ apart from the people who misused his name, to the difference between forgiveness and trust, what a healthy church looks like if you ever want one, and a faith that has outlived the people who misrepresented it. It will never ask you to go back to that church, to meet anyone who hurt you, or to keep quiet, and it sets no deadline on any decision about church or faith, in either direction. You can walk all eight weeks without setting foot in a church, and if you've stopped believing because of what happened, you're welcome to walk it anyway.

It is not a cure, and it is not a substitute for a doctor, a licensed counselor, a pastor you trust from another church, or the real people who believe you. If abuse or a crime is part of what happened, week one starts with safety and reporting, and that comes before everything else here. If what happened has brought you to thoughts of ending your life, call or text 988 before you go any further. Walk the plan imperfectly. A missed week is not failure; you just pick it back up. Some weeks the most faithful thing you can do will be to rest.
careNote: If what happened has taken over your sleep or your closest relationships, or panic, nightmares, or numbness have lasted for weeks, see a licensed counselor experienced with trauma who has no tie to that church. In a crisis, call or text 988, and if anyone is in danger now, call 911.

weeks.focus: Naming what happened, and getting safe
weeks.why: Church hurt comes in more than one shape, and the first work is to name yours at its real size. A careless word or a decision you disagreed with can hurt, and that's the ordinary cost of living among sinners. Spiritual abuse is different in kind: God's name or a leader's position used to control you, silence you, or shield someone who did harm. Some of what happens in churches is also a crime, whatever the church calls it, and a crime belongs with the police, not only the church. Reporting a crime done to you is your decision, and no one in that church gets to make it for you. Time limits differ by state and by crime, so ask a victim advocate or a lawyer before assuming it's too late. This isn't legal advice.
weeks.practice: If anyone is in danger now, call 911. If a child may be at risk, call the police or your state's child abuse hotline; you don't need proof or anyone's permission. If you're under eighteen and an adult is hurting you, tell a teacher, a school counselor, or another adult you trust. If you fear someone at home, call or text the Domestic Violence Hotline on Find Help. Each day, write one plain sentence about what was done; keep it where no one who hurt you can find it.

read.label: The church hurt me, the care page this plan walks beside, with what to do if a crime was committed

tool.label: The Find Help page, with 988, the Domestic Violence Hotline, and RAINN for sexual abuse, whenever it happened

weeks.reflection: What was done to me, called by its real name, and is anyone still in danger from the person who did it?

weeks.why: You may not be able to pray right now without hearing the voice that used prayer on you. The Psalms can lend you words until your own come back. Psalm 55 bears David's name, and the one praying it has been betrayed by a close friend he once worshiped beside: "We shared sweet fellowship together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God" (Psalm 55:14). Before he names the betrayal, he names the wish to get away: "Oh, that I had wings like a dove" (Psalm 55:6). If part of you has said you're done with all of it, the Bible has room for that, prayed aloud to God rather than confessed as a sin. Then the psalm runs from the betrayer toward God and tells him everything, anger included. That is lament, a faith that refuses to lie to God about what happened in his house.
weeks.practice: Each day, read Psalm 55 aloud, slowly, and mark the lines that are true for you. Pray those lines as your own, then tell God in one plain sentence what you want him to do. If this psalm is too close to the bone, pray Psalm 13 instead. Five minutes is enough, and on the days you can't pray at all, reading it as someone else's prayer still counts.

read.label: How to Practice Lament, on saying the complaint to God without softening it

tool.label: Psalm 55 in the Study Bible, with notes on the friend he once walked with to the house of God

weeks.reflection: What have I been afraid to say to God about what was done to me in his name?

weeks.why: Spiritual abuse depends on silence, and for some people the deeper wound came after they told, when the people in charge protected the one who did harm. So choose someone outside that church, with nothing to protect: a friend, a relative, a counselor, or a pastor from another church. In John 9 a man Jesus had healed kept telling the plain truth to authorities who wanted his story to go away. His own parents were afraid to stand with him (John 9:22), and in the end the authorities threw him out. Then the chapter turns: "When Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, He found the man" (John 9:35). If the first person you tell shrugs it off, that tells you about them, not about you. Try someone else.
weeks.practice: Each day this week, add a few lines to a private account of what happened: what was said and done, when, who was there, and who knew. Notes made close to the time can steady you if anyone insists you're remembering it wrong, and they can help if you ever report. If writing it stirs up more than you can carry, stop and do it with a counselor. Before the week ends, tell one safe person in plain words, or let them read the page.

read.label: Church Hurt, on telling the truth to God and to one safe person without softening it

tool.label: John 9 in the Study Bible, the man who kept telling the truth, was thrown out, and was found by Jesus

weeks.reflection: Who is one person outside that church who would believe me, and what am I afraid will happen if I tell them?

weeks.focus: When God's words were used as a leash
weeks.why: This wound goes deep because it came in God's name. Spiritual abuse works with true words, like submission, unity, and forgiveness, bent into a leash, so the Scripture and prayer you'd reach for to heal are the very things that cut. You may have heard a leader shielded with a line about not touching God's anointed. It comes from Psalm 105, where God guarded a few wandering families from the kings around them: "He rebuked kings on their behalf" (Psalm 105:14). A verse that protected the weak from the powerful was turned into a guard for the powerful. I'm a pastor, so I can't say this from outside it. Every pastor holds a trust that can be bent this way, and many of us have been quicker to preach submission than to submit to correction.
weeks.practice: Each day, write down one verse or church phrase that still makes you flinch. Then read the whole passage around it: who said it, to whom, and why. Write one line on what it meant there and one on how it was used on you. If a passage is too raw to read alone yet, set it aside for a day when you have company.

read.label: Submitting to Leaders, on why Scripture binds the shepherd harder than the sheep

tool.label: The Passage Context tool, opened to the psalm behind the line about not touching God's anointed

weeks.reflection: Which verse still sounds like the voice that used it on me, and have I ever read it where it actually stands?

weeks.focus: Telling Christ apart from those who used his name
weeks.why: Underneath it all may run a question you haven't said aloud: was God in on it too? Scripture is fiercer toward shepherds who harm the flock than the church that hurt you may ever have been. Through Ezekiel, God charged Israel's shepherds, "you have ruled them with violence and cruelty" (Ezekiel 34:4), then set himself against them and went looking for the scattered sheep himself. Jesus condemned leaders who "tie up heavy, burdensome loads and lay them on men's shoulders" (Matthew 23:4), and at the end of the same speech he longed to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her chicks. But this distinction can't become the church's alibi. When Jesus set himself apart from the religious leaders of his day, it wasn't to let them off. It was to judge them.
weeks.practice: Read the Gospel of Mark, a chapter a day, as if you'd never heard of Jesus. Keep three short lists as you go: whom he touches, whom he defends, and whom he confronts. Notice where the people who hurt you would have stood in those stories, and where Jesus would have found you.

read.label: When It All Comes Apart, a Bible study, session three: When the Church Is the Reason

tool.label: Mark 1 in the Study Bible, to begin the Gospel a chapter a day with notes on its setting

weeks.reflection: When I picture God, whose face do I see, and does it look more like the people who hurt me or like the Jesus I'm meeting in Mark?

weeks.why: Forgiveness is one of the true words most easily bent into a leash, as if forgiving meant going back, trusting again, or never speaking of it. It never meant any of that. Forgiveness, when it comes, hands the debt to God, who judges rightly (Romans 12:19). Trust is a different thing, rebuilt slowly by truth told and behavior changed, and sometimes never. Reconciliation takes two people and real repentance, which is why Paul's counsel carries two honest conditions: "If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone" (Romans 12:18). With some people it isn't possible, and that isn't your failure. You can forgive and still report a crime, keep your distance for life, and never set foot in that church again. No one should ever ask you to meet with someone who abused you.
weeks.practice: Fold a page into three columns headed forgive, trust, and contact. Under each, write honestly where you are with the person who hurt you, and with the church if it protected them. Each day, pray one sentence handing God a piece of the debt, even if all you can say is that you can't yet. This week is for deciding, not for contacting anyone.

read.label: How Do You Heal After Betrayal by Someone Close? On forgiveness, reconciliation, and trust, three different things

tool.label: I can't forgive them, the care page that keeps forgiving, trusting, and contact apart

weeks.reflection: Can I hand God the debt and still keep my distance, and who taught me those two couldn't go together?

weeks.focus: What a safe church looks like, whenever you're ready
weeks.why: You may not walk into a church during these eight weeks, or for a long while after, and this plan doesn't need you to. Still, it helps to know what a healthy church looks like while your eyes are open, so that if you ever try again, you're looking for what's hard to fake. Its leaders answer to people who can tell them no, and they welcome questions. Money and decisions are handled in the open. It can tell you plainly what it does when someone reports abuse, and it speaks of people who left with respect. The charge to elders in 1 Peter is a fair test: "not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock" (1 Peter 5:3). Belonging can start small, with one or two Christians you trust, reading Scripture and praying with you.
weeks.practice: Each day, add one line to a private list of what a church would have to show you before you could trust it. If you aren't ready to visit, the list is the whole practice, and it counts. If you are, visit one church more than once, sit near the door, leave whenever you need to, and ask what it does when someone reports abuse.

read.label: How Do You Find a Church Worth Joining? What to forgive, what to flee, and how to visit without promising anything

tool.label: 1 Peter 5 in the Study Bible, the charge to elders to lead willingly and by example, not by lording it over anyone

weeks.reflection: What would a church have to show me before I could trust it, and who could I read and pray with in the meantime?

weeks.why: A wound like this can leave you wondering whether any of it was real. If your faith was in Christ, it never rested on the people who pointed you to him. Soon after the man in John 9 was thrown out, Jesus spoke to the same leaders about thieves and hired hands and a shepherd whose sheep know his voice, and later he said of his sheep, "No one can snatch them out of My hand" (John 10:28). The people who hurt you could close a door. They couldn't take you out of his hand. What has come through these weeks may be smaller and quieter than the faith you started with, and more your own. Guard it from turning hard, and ask God to keep this wound from making you into someone who wounds.
weeks.practice: Write on a card the two or three practices from these weeks that actually helped, maybe a psalm in the morning, a chapter of Mark, or one person who knows the truth. Keep them each day. Then write down one true thing that has outlasted the people who taught it to you, and keep it with the card for the hard mornings.

read.label: John 10 in the Study Bible, the good shepherd whose sheep know his voice, set against thieves and hired hands

tool.label: The Rule of Life Builder, to choose only the rhythms you can keep now, like daily Scripture and one trusted friend

weeks.reflection: What has outlasted the people who misrepresented God to me, and how will I keep it now that it's mine?
